# Preface.

---

The title of these manuscripts shows what can be expected here, and identifies the readers for whom they are actually intended. I yielded to the wishes of many of my friends and acquaintances when I decided to allow them to appear publicly before the audience.

These are writings that a series of very diligent researchers of the secret sciences <note>The term "secret sciences" (geheime Wissenschaften) refers to occult and esoteric studies, such as alchemy, Hermeticism, and natural magic, which were highly regarded in the courts of the 16th and 17th centuries.</note> brought together over the course of nearly 200 years.

Emperor Rudolph <note>Rudolf II (1552–1612), Holy Roman Emperor, was a well-known patron of the occult and alchemy, transforming his court in Prague into a center for esoteric research.</note> and his successor Matthias are the first who laid the foundation for this collection. Hertod, the Chief Physician <term>Archiater: A title for a personal physician to a monarch or high-ranking official.</term> to Emperor Leopold I, continued it; the Baron von Engels- <meta>The catchword "hardt" indicates the name is Engelshardt.</meta>

them speak their own language, even if it is a dialect that has gone out of fashion or <term>barbaric Latin: A term for medieval or non-classical Latin often used by scholars and occultists that did not adhere to strict Roman grammatical rules.</term>. This, however, applies primarily to the actual alchemical and magical works, for in them <term>kabbalistic transposition: The practice of rearranging letters or words to reveal or hide mystical meanings.</term> or <term>steganographic masking: The art of hiding a secret message within an ordinary-looking text.</term> is something very common.

I have seen that through certain "beautifications" of this kind, it is not uncommon for an entire work to become incomprehensible. Its embedded secret—whether real or intended, that does not matter here—is wiped away, and now nothing remains of all that which was, in fact, not very hidden in the original.

The division of each volume shall be sevenfold. The beginning will always be made by a preface or introduction, in which I will sometimes say something in general about writings of this kind, but at other times I will stay only with what occurs in the specific volume provided, providing what can serve as either a history or an explanation of its contents.

# Preliminary Report

I have indicated in the preface how extensively I intend to divide each volume; according to this plan, the present preliminary report thus constitutes the **First Division** of it.

In this section, I will provide various accounts of the writings that appear in this volume; I will take the liberty of making several remarks as they arise from the subjects at hand, and, alongside the judgment of a connoisseur <note>original: "Kunstbesitzers," literally an owner of art or knowledge, likely a collector</note> regarding alchemical writings, I will also include some anecdotes pertaining to the history of the art <note>referring to the "Hermetic Art" or alchemy</note> and of this man.

The second division contains:

1. A treatise on lead-glass work <term>lead-glass work: the craft of producing glass with lead oxide, used for its brilliance and in the creation of artificial gemstones</term>.

2. The preparation of carmine <term>carmine: a prized deep-red pigment derived from cochineal insects</term> and carmine ink.

3. A remedy against bone cancer <note>historically "Beinkrebs" could refer to various bone diseases, including necrosis or severe infections, as well as malignancy</note>.

4. Several very effective medicines for intermittent fevers <term>intermittent fevers: a term historically used for cyclical fevers such as malaria</term>.

### 7. Monte-Snyder’s [Treatise] on the Universal Medicine and the *Metamorphosis of the Planets* <note>original: "Montesny der Universalmedizin und Metamorphosis Planetarum"</note>.

However, it is certain that he knew the destruction of metals <note>The process of "killing" or dissolving a metal to release its inner spirit.</note> and taught the simplification of the otherwise difficult fermentation and metallic specification very thoroughly; otherwise, it has not yet been irrefutably proven that he did not also understand the Great Work <note>The *Magnum Opus*, the full process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> itself, as very many passages here can be interpreted as such without being forced.

...tapped and collected in barrels; likewise, where **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> is depicted standing, but **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturnus"</note> is winged, these are particularly noteworthy. They confirm, contrary to generally accepted opinion, the fixity of Mercury and the volatility of Saturn <note>In traditional alchemy, Mercury is usually the "volatile" principle (fluid and changing) while Saturn/Lead is "fixed" (heavy and sluggish). The author notes that Flamel’s imagery reverses this, suggesting a specialized stage of the process where the properties are swapped.</note>. Regarding the **serpent on the cross**, and the cross that appears so frequently among alchemists, there remains this very special observation: there is a body whose sediment, after the moisture has evaporated, constantly reveals itself in the shape of a cross. It can thus serve as a sure sign that the artist is on the right path and possesses at least a portion of the Art when this sign appears in his labors. The application of this, and how he may make his own the serpent to be fixed thereto, as well as the earth in which the cross is seen placed, are subjects that provide as much occupation for the contemplation of the natural philosopher as they serve as sources of joy once he has mastered the meaning of these **hieroglyphs** <note>In the 17th and 18th centuries, "hieroglyphs" referred to any symbolic or mystical image, particularly the famous "Hieroglyphic Figures" attributed to Nicolas Flamel.</note>. What is otherwise claimed of Flamel—that he still lives <note>There was a persistent legend that Nicolas Flamel discovered the Elixir of Life and was still living in the East centuries after his recorded death in 1418.</note>—can be determined with as little certainty as the claim that his entire history is merely a parable devised to conceal the Art.

### 10. Khunrath.

Everything by him is rare. The *German Purgatory* <note>original: "Das deutsche Fegfeuer." This refers to a specific polemical text or a metaphorical critique of the era.</note> says of him that he wrote not from the Spirit of God, but from the ignorant <term>spirit of pride</term>; <note>original: "unwissenden Hoffahrtsteufel." The "Hoffahrtsteufel" was a popular religious trope in 16th-century literature used to personify the sin of vanity and arrogance.</note> and even if not much—and at most only a part—of the great secret of nature can be learned from his writings, there is nonetheless no falsehood presented within them, and that in itself is an advantage for a seeker of the Art. He claims, it is true, that he possesses the science of the Art <note>Alchemy</note>, and also that he has witnessed its practical elaboration; and although a real and essential part of the Art can indeed be learned from him, there is yet no trace of the degree of the most hidden parts of it in his writi-

The 5th [Key] is one of the most distinguished; the figures appearing therein are of the most important significance. In general, there is even more to be learned from the illustrations than from the text, for in those, he is at least not as reserved as he is in his explanations.

As proof of this, consider the 12th Key, where in the illustration, the fermentation <note>In alchemy, fermentation is the process of "ripening" the stone or medicine by adding a specific substance to give it power.</note> is correctly represented, but in the text, it is taught quite falsely, despite the fact that Basil promised to proceed quite candidly therein. One should adhere least to the literal meaning with this author; rather, he is not infrequently to be understood and interpreted in the exact opposite way. Thus, for example, he teaches: that the purification should occur through fire, and yet he intends to indicate thereby that it must be performed with water. He has specified the matter by name. *The Birth of the Planets* is full of allegory and kabbalistic transposition <note>original: "kabbalistischer Versetzung." This refers to the practice of rearranging letters or symbols to hide a secret meaning, common in esoteric Jewish and alchemical traditions.</note>.

4th. reduces it <note>In metallurgy, "reduction" is the process of using heat and a "combustible" (like charcoal) to turn a metal oxide back into a pure metal.</note> with the appropriate combustibles, which the artists call *ineriren* <note>Likely a specialized metallurgical term for "incorporating" or "fixing" the metal during the reduction process.</note>; thus, from this restored lead, the aforementioned portion—namely, the fourth part—of very gold-bearing silver shall be obtained.

Furthermore, the work is greatly eased by the stamp mills <term>stamp mills: "Pochwerke," heavy machinery used to crush ore into powder.</term>, and the firing <note>The fuel used for the furnaces.</note> also does not cost much.

### Preparation of the Crucibles.

One takes <term>Hessian crucibles: "Dutenflaschen," specifically the triangular-shaped ceramic vessels famously made in Grossalmerode.</term> crushed small, pure fat <note>In this context, "fat" refers to clay that is rich and plastic, rather than sandy.</note> well-washed loam that is not sandy, finely washed <term>cupel ash: "Testasche," the ash used to make cupels for refining precious metals.</term> which is also not sandy, and <term>feather-white: "Federweiß," a historical term for fibrous minerals like talc or amianthus (asbestos) used for heat resistance.</term>, all in equal weight. These are finely powdered and mixed with good strong beer and egg white, which have been well beaten together. This mixture is made as thin as painters are accustomed to make their paints. A warmed crucible that has no iron stains is then coated with this using a brush, allowed to dry, and this process is repeated several times; thus, one can be certain that no <term>lead-glass: "Bleyglaß," referring here to molten litharge or lead oxide, which is highly corrosive and easily soaks through porous ceramic.</term> will penetrate them.

This instruction for smelting vessels, which perform everything they promise, is entirely accurate. The artist from whom I received it was a potter in **Goslar** by the **Harz**, who held the contract for supplying the <term>cupels: "Kapellen," small, porous bowls used in assaying to separate precious metals from lead.</term> for the mining towns of the Harz, **Clausthal**, **Zellerfeld**, and several other works. I would never have suspected in a man of his station the knowledge he possessed of the <term>arts of refining and smelting: "Scheide- und Schmelzkunst."</term> I could have found no better guide than this brave man, who led me through a portion of the Harz Mountains in the year 1763; I heard from him the most singular reports of these mountains and many types of ore which, as yet unmined, are only sought out and utilized by those with true knowledge.

<meta>This page continues the author's discussion of metallurgical techniques, moving from the physical preparation of crucibles to the specific chemical use of lead-glass (litharge) in the refining of precious metals. On this occasion, the variety of materials also led him to **lead-glass works**. His opinion of these notorious operations was far removed from everything other writers had said about them. He viewed them from two perspectives.

He cited the first as nothing more than a purer and better <term>method of separation: "Scheidungsart," the process of refining gold and silver from base metals or ores.</term>, whereby the gold- and silver-like parts scattered in rocks, earths, and metals are brought closer together. Through <term>slagging: "Verschlacken," the process of turning impurities into a glassy waste product (slag) to isolate the metal.</term>, the lighter or more <term>refractory: "strengflüssigere," referring to materials that are difficult to melt or fuse.</term> earths are separated from the metal. In this way, somewhat more is obtained than through ordinary separation; however, the profit from this would rarely be enough to amass great riches.

The second perspective, of which the alchemists treat and at which the **"Great and Small Bauer"** <note>This likely refers to "Der dreyfache philosophische Radix im großen und kleinen Bauer," a famous alchemical text published by Johann Gottfried Jugel in 1744.</note> aims, likely occurs through properly prepared, "unlocked" metals. In this case, the <term>lead-glass: "Bleyglaß," here referring to molten lead oxide or litharge used as a flux.</term> is merely a means to cover these prepared metals and protect them from <term>evaporating: "Ausrauchen," literally "smoking out," referring to the loss of material through volatilization during heating.</term> before they have completed their effect in the melting silver and fully "ripened" <note>original: "ausgezeitiget." In alchemy, "ripening" refers to the perceived maturation of "imperfect" metals into gold.</note> its gold-like parts. 

In this latter way, he believes that lead-glass works yield rich separations and can be carried out with great profit. However, what is commonly claimed about this is nothing but empty conjecture, arising from a lack of suitable <note>The text ends mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

## First Experiment.
### With common pebble and litharge.

He had the kindness to convince me through actual experiments that the <term>lead-glass: "Bleyglas," a molten flux created from lead oxide.</term> would be preserved without the slightest damage in a prepared melting crucible through a three-day intense smelting fire. After the <term>reduction: "Redukzion," the chemical process of returning a metal oxide to its metallic state.</term>, he showed me how little trust should be placed in the writers who have written about these works, and that once the fuel costs are deducted, instead of profit, only a loss always results, unless one obtains an advantage through the <term>additive: "Zuschlag," material added to a melt to facilitate the separation of metals.</term> of special <term>types of minerals: "Bergarten," literally "mountain-types," referring to various ores or rocky minerals.</term> which cannot be expected from raw metals. Some minerals, however, which contain nothing according to the ordinary <term>methods of separation: "Scheidungsarten," the standard refining processes used to isolate gold and silver from ore.</term>, might finally reveal a content through a sustained melting with lead-glass that pays for the effort and costs; and he also proved this at that very time with a <term>clay: "Lette," a fatty, often colorful clay or loam found in mineral veins.</term> that is found <term>at the surface: "am Tage," literally "at the day," a mining term for minerals found at or near the ground level.</term> above Harzburg <note>A significant mining town in the Harz Mountains of Germany, famous for its silver and lead production.</note>.

## Sixth Experiment.

Another experiment belongs here, which Mr. Anton Pettersch—a skilled <term>pyrotechnician: "Feuerkündiger," literally "one knowledgeable in fire," referring to a specialist in assaying or smelting.</term>—conducted with Danube sand.

Using a simple lead glass, which he had made from 3 parts <term>minium: "Mennig," red lead oxide used as a flux.</term> and 1 part white sand, he obtained 18 grains of gold through 12 hours of melting.

From that same sand another time [he obtained] 11 grains of gold; and from the stones found in quarries along the Danube above Nußdorf <note>A village near Vienna, now part of the city's 19th district.</note>, he also obtained 8 to 10 grains of gold.

And from other stones on the Kahlenberg <note>A hill in the Vienna Woods overlooking the Danube, famous for its views of the city.</note>, about 1/2 <term>Quintlein: "Quent," a unit of weight.</term> of silver, but no gold.

## Seventh [Author's] Own Experiment with Danube Sand.

I performed the same experiment with Danube sand from the exact same location where Mr. P * <note>Referring to Anton Pettersch.</note> had taken his; the experiment was conducted with total precision in the presence of us both, and we obtained from it not a trace of either gold or silver. This experiment was repeated several more times, and the result was exactly the same.

From all these experiments presented so far, it is now evident that the judgment of Mr. Ensign <note>original: "Herrn Fähndrichs." For the first, third, and seventh experiments are perfectly identical to one another and prove that no actual gold and silver particles are found within the materials chosen for these works, nor is any gold or silver obtained by melting with <term>lead glass: "Bleyglas," a flux made of lead oxides and silica, used in assaying to separate metals.</term>; and that all those authors who assured us of such great advantages from the long-enduring meltings of lead glass have, due to a lack of suitable <note>The author implies that poorly made crucibles or vessels may have introduced impurities, leading earlier researchers to false conclusions.</note> vessels, deceived themselves and others; and if they did indeed obtain actual improvements through such works, these must be attributed not to the lead glass, but to the admixture of other prepared or even unprepared materials, as is confirmed by the remaining experiments.

The second and sixth experiments further show that, with the help of lead glass, the gold and silver-like particles found in sand and <term>rock types: "Bergarten," referring to various minerals or ore-bearing stones.</term> are brought closer together, and thus noble metals can be separated from them in this way, which otherwise would emerge from them with difficulty or not at all.

Finally, from the fourth and fifth experiments, one sees the possibility that by combining <term>substances: "Körpern," literally "bodies," used here in the archaic sense of chemical or physical matter.</term>, noble metals and others of their kind are produced which are not to be found individually in any of them; however, regarding these latter two, I always assume that they actually occurred correctly, exactly as they were reported.

# Augmentation of Gold
# <note>original: "Augmentum Solis"</note>

Received from Mr. Balthasar Albinus, Councilor to the Elector of Cologne, which he shared with me out of Christian love and clearly demonstrated.

Take common yellow <term>sulfur</term> <note>symbol: $\triangle$</note>, pulverize it, put it into a glass, and pour a strong <term>acid</term> <note>original: "$\nabla$," symbols for water or aqua fortis/acid</note> upon it. Let it cool, then pour the <term>acid</term> back onto it and draw it off once more. Do this four times. Crush and grind the <term>residue</term> <note>original: "todten Kopf" or *caput mortuum*, the dregs remaining after distillation</note>, and set it to dissolve on a glass dish in a damp cellar. In this way, the sulfur dissolves into an oil. <term>Purify</term> <note>original: "rectificire"</note> this with fresh spring water using a retort, and separate the water from the oil using a small funnel. Let it circulate, and it will become as red as a ruby; it can be used internally and externally without any corrosive effect.

Now take one mark of laminated silver <note>silver beaten into thin sheets</note>, make small rolls out of it, and pour the oil of sulfur over it so that it completely covers the <term>silver</term> <note>symbol: $\☽$ / Luna</note>. Place a blind alembic <note>a still-head without a spout, used to force vapors back down</note> on the flask and let it digest in warm ashes for 14 days. In this way, the <term>silver</term> will be eaten away by the oil, and will become like—

### Number 25.

->§. 31. Under the Title: *From the Field of Mars.* <note>original: "Ex Campo Martis." In alchemy, Mars is the symbol for iron; this title suggests a procedure related to the properties or "essentials" of iron.</note><-

->*Communicated by Dr. Ludolph Dom. Weiß.*<-

Take ½ lb of iron or copper sheet; place it in a new glazed pot with ½ lb of sulfur *layered one upon the other* <term>S. S. S.: abbreviation for *stratum super stratum*, a technique of layering materials in a crucible</term>. Seal another pot on top with lute <note>a clay-based cement used to make airtight seals on laboratory vessels</note>, in which a small hole the width of a finger has been made at the top. Place this in a circular fire <note>a furnace arrangement where heat surrounds the vessel</note> for 3 hours, but ensure that the sulfur does not ignite, but rather only slowly evaporates. Finally, increase the fire so that the entire pot glows red, then let everything cool. Take out the metal sheets, which will be completely swollen and so brittle that one can break them with a finger. Grind these into a fine powder; boil this powder in an iron pan with filtered rainwater for a good hour. Pour the water away, and into the dried powder, mix and rub 4 Loth <note>a traditional German unit of weight; 4 Loth is approximately 60 grams or 2 ounces</note> of salmiac <term>Salmiac: ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to "open" or dissolve metals</term> thoroughly together. Carry this powdered mass onto a **refining dish** <term>Treibscherben: a shallow, heat-resistant ceramic vessel used for roasting or refining ores</term>, which must be so warm that it almost glows. Stir the mixture constantly with an iron shovel, and the salmiac will melt and break open the metallic **bodies** <note>original: "Corpora"; refers to the physical substance of the metal</note> like water; let the material remain with constant stirring for as long as

### No. 27.

### §. 86. *Saffron of Mars.* <note>original: Crocus Martis; a term for iron oxide, typically a reddish powder produced by calcining iron</note>

When iron is sublimated <term>sublimirt: heated until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</term> 3 or 4 times with **mercury sublimate** <term>Sublimat: corrosive sublimate or mercury(II) chloride</term>, and each time ground back into the dregs <note>original: fæces</note>, it becomes so beautiful that it is a wonder to behold, and it easily permeates into silver.

Now take pure and crystalline **mercury sublimate** <term>Mercurii Sublimati: mercury(II) chloride, a highly toxic white salt</term> and the best **Hungarian antimony** <note>original: Antimonii hungarici; antimony from Hungary was highly prized by alchemists for its supposed purity and high mineral "sulfur" content</note>. Then dissolve **borax** <term>boracem: a mineral salt used as a flux in soldering and metallurgy</term> in **spirit of wine** <term>Spiritu Vini: concentrated ethanol or high-proof alcohol</term>, grind the stone finely and sprinkle it with the prescribed borax-water, dry it, and repeat this three times. If this treatise had not already grown larger through the attached **metal preparations** <note>original: Metallzurichtungen; refers to the chemical treatment and refinement of metals</note> than I had initially intended, I would have added several more instructions to the current ones, which have a close relationship with them and are recorded in the *Selected Treasury* <note>original: *Thesaurus selectus*</note>.

Only a few more remarks about some of these metal preparations remain for me, which I do not wish to withhold from the lovers of the **higher art of separation** <term>Scheidekunst: literally "the art of separation," a contemporary term for chemistry or alchemy</term>.

Among them, I will say nothing new, or nothing that they have not already encountered themselves in one way or another; however, as a writer, I also have to deal with the *uninitiated masses, and the common folk of every kind, and all men* <note>original Latin: *vulgus profanum & omnis generis vulgus & hominibus*</note>, who are even more diverse than their own faces. I must deal with truly enlightened great men, whose gaze strives toward the very bottom of things, but who—where they are unable to see all the way to the end—candidly admit it with a modesty like that of <term>Boerhaave</term> <note>Herman Boerhaave (1668–1738) was a world-renowned Dutch physician and chemist, famous for his humility and for establishing the modern system of clinical teaching.</note>, and conclude with <term>Shakespeare</term> <note>A reference to the famous line from *Hamlet*: "There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy."</note> that there may well be many other things under the moon of which our philosophy has not dreamed a single syllable.

Likewise, I stand before the judgment seat of the "little men of light" <note>likely a satirical reference to narrow-minded Rationalists or self-proclaimed "enlightened" thinkers of the era</note> who cannot see the sun because of its very brilliance, and yet are able to correctly and vigorously split every one of their own dust motes. I have to deal with "heads and torsos" <note>perhaps referring to incomplete or fragmented thinkers who lack a holistic view</note>, with the weak-minded who see miracles and goblins everywhere where simple, everyday observations could provide clarity; and with those "fear-mongers" to whom God and <term>Alchemy</term> <note>The ancient art of transmuting base metals into gold and seeking universal medicines, which the author views as a serious spiritual and physical science.</note>, Christ and the spirit world are just as much platitudes as divine revelation. To them, any insight into the future—which extends just a span further than their noses—is something they have been unable to reach even with their <term>lorgnette</term> <note>A pair of spectacles held by a handle, used here metaphorically for the artificial and limited tools of "modern" critics.</note>. With these and a hundred variations of them, I must contend.

and to all of these, I wish to tell what follows:

Many of the <term>particular works</term> <note>In alchemy, "particular works" refer to processes intended to transmute specific base metals into gold or silver, as opposed to the "Universal" work of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> and metallic operations recorded here are literally true, based on the repeated experience of the most insightful <term>masters of separation</term> <note>From the German *Scheidekünstler*, referring to experts in assaying and the chemical separation of metals.</note>, and they do everything that is claimed of them. That is the one side! And the other: These very same true experiments, established through experience and lucrative, performed with the very same materials, with the very same degrees of fire, with the very same caution, and worked by those very same insightful masters of separation—is it not true that they then fail to do what is claimed of them? They do much today, little tomorrow, even less the day after, and then nothing at all; they do something again, and then nothing again, and so on until—all at once they do everything again, and even more than was expected. And now—everyone is full of joy, full of gold! Now the right causes have been found, the right manipulations achieved; now it can never fail again; now one performs it again according to this "certain method," and now—and this certain method yields—not even a trace! Perhaps one of the additives did not have the proper quality this time, and so it [disappears/dwindles]...

In the other procedures involving silver, and the associated so-called **gradations** <term>gradations: "Gradierungen," chemical processes intended to improve the quality, color, or density of a metal, often to make it more like gold.</term> from No. 7 to 16, **lime** <term>lime: "Kalk," specifically quicklime or calcium oxide, which was used in early chemistry for its high reactivity and caustic nature.</term> is everywhere prescribed in heavy weight. "Volatile" suggests a preparation that could be distilled or that gave off strong vapors.</term> already noted; yet, no mention is made therein that this experiment belongs to those which succeed at one time, but then refuse to work again at another.

In several manuscripts in my collection, a similar effect is ascribed to volatile liver of sulfur. Among others, however, it is found in **Johann Georg Hofmann’s** manuscript, which stands under No. 22 in the ***Catalogue of Manuscripts*** <note>original: "Catalogus Manuscriptorum."</note>. In its second part, on page 156, under the title ***The Old Gentleman's Specific Procedure*** <note>original: "Particular des alten Herrn." In alchemy, a "particular" refers to a recipe intended to achieve a specific chemical transformation, such as refining a particular metal, rather than the "universal" goal of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, is the preparation of a volatile liver of sulfur that will follow immediately. Included herewith is the original letter of a certain **von Zisla**, who provides more specific details on the matter. However, it also contains the observation that this work did not even once show the same success as the other, and that nine experiments conducted with it yielded a different result every time. Yet I record both here for the sake of their strangeness, and indeed in their own words.

Regarding the **silver treatment** <term>silver treatment: "Silberzurichtung," referring to the specific chemical or physical preparation of silver for use in further experiments.</term> noted under No. 6, it has already been stated above that it is very frequently referred to in the remaining volumes of the ***Selected Treasury*** <note>original: "Thesaurus selectus." This likely refers to a specific collection of alchemical or chemical recipes.</note>. In those volumes, it is intended to serve as a processed and perfectly pure silver, all the better to absorb the effects of other metallic preparations.

In the other treatments of silver, and the associated so-called **gradations** <term>gradations: "Gradierungen," chemical processes intended to improve the quality, color, or purity of a metal, often through repeated heating or specific additives.</term> from No. 7 to 16, **lime** <term>lime: "Kalk," here referring to calx or calcium oxide, a common reagent in early chemistry used as a flux or for purification.</term> is prescribed in heavy weight throughout. The variety of the lime, whether it was burned strongly or weakly, the time that has elapsed between its burning and its use, the vapors in whose vicinity it has been kept, the season, and the weather—none of these are to be disregarded in experiments of this kind. They can produce very noticeable changes in the results, and outcomes quite different from what one expects. The discrepancies observed in experiments, which even the most skilled **assayers** <term>assayers: "Scheidekünstler," literally "parting artists," historical chemists specializing in the separation, testing, and refining of precious metals.</term> have been unable to explain or avoid, perhaps depend on some of these environmental circumstances.

### Against tertian fever <note>original: "Contra febrem tertianam." A tertian fever is one where the paroxysms or fever spikes occur every third day (counting the day of the fever, one day of rest, and then the next fever day), typical of certain types of malaria.</note>

**Oil of Scorpions** <note>original: "Oleum Scorpionum." *Criterion.* Professor a * * * *; let faith rest with the authors <note>original: "fit fides penes Authores." This is a common scholarly disclaimer of the time, suggesting that the reliability of the claim depends on the original authorities cited.</note>.

## No. 3.

# A salt that laxes and cures intermittent fevers.

If one presses out the soft pith from juniper wood, and then fills it with salt and burns it to charcoal, the salt melts within it.

This salt purges <term>purgiret</term> <note>Acts as a laxative to "cleanse" the body of ill humors.</note> in a small dose, and heals intermittent fevers <term>Wechselfieber</term> <note>Also known as "ague," these are fevers where the temperature rises and falls at regular intervals, typically indicative of malaria.</note>.

**Critique.** Nothing special at all, so it seems, or it would have to be proven through practical experience.

### No. 8.
# Fever Remedy of the Jesuits in Tyrnau.

The discovery of this remedy belongs to the late Reinsperger, of whom I have already spoken on another occasion.

During a journey he made to Hungary, he came to <term>Tyrnau</term>, <note>Now Trnava in modern-day Slovakia; it was a significant Jesuit educational and cultural center in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note> where, during a period of widespread fevers, he heard of a fever powder that the Jesuits distributed in their pharmacy, and of the general relief it provided even when the science of the physicians was at its wit's end. He therefore went to the pharmacy himself, had some items shown to him and others given to him, and arranged meanwhile for someone to be sent to fetch the fever powder.

---

Note. Some wish to hold that the following treatise was written by Doctor Thomas Aquinas <note>original: "Thoma Aquino"; a hugely influential 13th-century theologian. While several alchemical texts bear his name, most are considered "pseudo-epigrapha"—works written by others using his famous name to gain authority.</note> in Rome.

---

Behold, true Alchemy <term>Alchemia (the art of transmuting base metals into gold and seeking spiritual perfection)</term> is an imitator of nature, as Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a teacher of Aquinas and a renowned scholar of natural science who was often cited as an authority in alchemical texts.</note> says, and it is entirely founded and built upon the preparation of natural things. To know their cause and foundation is necessary for those who do not wish to go astray in this art. First of all, it is essential to recognize the natural constitution and the form <note>original Latin: "Formam"; in medieval philosophy, the "form" is the internal principle that gives a substance its specific identity.</note> of things, because from these two parts all natural things have their being. Afterward, one must understand the workings of nature in such a way that he may govern <note>original: "geregiren", meaning to direct or rule one's actions.</note> and conduct himself accordingly in his own operations.

Now, regarding the first point—the natural constitution of natural things—it is first to be recognized, in a general sense, how that

the wisdom of God has divided and separated the circles and stars of the whole world into two parts: into the natural world on the one hand, and the heavenly world on the other. The first is the circle of the four elements <term>four elements (the classical components of all matter: earth, water, air, and fire)</term>, beginning from the Earth up to the stars of the Moon <note>In medieval cosmology, the "sublunary sphere" (below the moon) was the realm of change and decay, composed of the four elements, while everything above the moon was eternal and unchanging.</note>, where the other world begins to extend up to the starry heaven. 

The first world was created first in a common, unformed matter <note>original: "ungebildeter Materie"; in alchemy, this is often called 'Prima Materia' or the first matter from which all things originate.</note>, so that the wisdom of God created an unformed matter about which both the pagan masters <note>original: "heidnische Meister"; likely referring to classical Greek philosophers such as Aristotle and Plato.</note> and the teachers of Holy Scripture write much. And He further divided such matter into four parts, and formed each one specifically with cold, heat, dryness, and moisture, so that because such qualities and forms—like heat and cold—are by nature against one another and cannot stand together in one, they were separated and divided into the aforementioned matter in four parts, called the four elements from the described matter, by means of adding heat, cold, etc. 

And all this was done so that all other natural things may henceforth possess their natural character <note>original: "Natürlichkeit"; the inherent essence or physical reality of a thing.</note> from such elements and creatures, by means of their being joined together. ...of the four elements <term>four elements (the classical components of all matter: earth, water, air, and fire)</term>. This is not to be understood as if the four elements gather together of their own accord, one into the place of another—no, for by its very nature, one element flees the place of another element. Rather, one element is compelled by heat, drawn and lifted into another, so that we never find any single element clear and pure on its own without the mixing of another. As a matter of truth, we always find earth to be dry only if it has moisture within it, and we also always find water unless there is some earthiness within it; this is clearly demonstrated in the distillation <term>distillation (the alchemical process of heating a substance to separate its components through evaporation and condensation)</term> of water. Likewise, the earth is rarely without internal heat.

It should be noted that in every single thing, only two elements appear visibly—namely water and earth—while two elements do not appear visibly but are hidden from the eyes. Thus, the heat—that is, the fire—is enclosed within the earth, and the air within the water. How this arrangement specifically works is not of great necessity to know here, but only that one should know that nature first prepared a common matter <term>common matter (often called 'materia prima', the base substance from which all specific things are made)</term> of things from the gathering together of the four elements. Nature adds to, arranges, and prepares this matter ever more skillfully; and the more subtle and skillfully such matter is prepared, the closer it is to its Form <note>In the philosophy of the time, "Form" was the spiritual or essential blueprint that turned raw "Matter" into a specific object, like a tree or a stone.</note>, or the more skillfully there shines forth from it the

In this way, the most pure mercury alone, without any coarse sulfurousness, fixes itself into gold. Thus, in this manner, we have a description of the natural generation <term>Geberunge: the process of "giving birth" to or creating a substance</term> of gold.

However, if it should happen that the mercury takes on certain impurities or encounters some kind of hindrance or defect—whether the heat is too great or too weak, or the place <note>original: "Stadt"; here referring to the "matrix" or specific location in the earth where the metal is forming</note> is impure and coarse, or if some other useless accident or hindrance occurs so that Nature cannot ultimately separate and cook away the impurities—then gold does not result. Because such impurity remains present, it becomes either copper or lead, iron or tin, depending on whether the impurity was cooked and digested much or little. 

Therefore, one finds that although such impurity and combustible sulfurousness are mixed and mingled together, this same combustible sulfurousness is not harmful to the mercury. The mercury itself does not burn from such sulfur; instead, the sulfur burns away on its own without burning the mercury with which it is mixed in these imperfect metals <term>unvollkommenen Metallen: base metals like lead or tin, which alchemists viewed as "unfinished" or "impure" versions of gold</term>.

So it is also with **Gold**: as long as it remains whole in its essence, it takes no strength or **seminal quality** <note>original: *Sämlichkeit*. The inherent "seed-like" ability of a substance to reproduce or grow.</note> into itself, for in that state it is not suitable or fit to receive such strength. But when it is brought back to its **first state** <note>original: *Standte*. Referring to the primal, undifferentiated condition of the metal before it became "fixed" as gold.</note>, to its most subtle nature, it then takes the power into itself. And so it may well be compared to growing things, and for that reason **Haly** <note>Likely referring to Haly Abenragel or Khalid ibn Yazid, influential figures in the transmission of Arabic alchemy to the Latin West.</note> says:

> This **Stone** rises up like a greening thing.

<meta>This page continues the argument for the transmutation of metals by highlighting the physical similarities between base metals and gold, contrasting them with organic materials like wood or stone.</meta>

the Tincture <term>Tincture <note>original: *Tinktur*. In alchemy, a "tincture" is a potent substance—often the Philosopher's Stone in liquid or powder form—capable of "coloring" or transforming base metals into gold by imbued them with its own perfect qualities.</note></term> in a short period. And since the imperfect metals <note>original: *unvollkommenen Metallen*. In the alchemical worldview, metals like lead, tin, copper, or iron were considered "sick" or unfinished versions of gold that simply needed the right conditions to reach perfection.</note> are so close to gold, as is clearly shown by certain properties they share with it—for just as gold is malleable <note>original: *schmeidig*. Meaning ductile, soft, or easy to shape.</note> and allows itself to be hammered and also cast, so too do the imperfect metals. This is a sign that they are very near to gold; and the more closely things correspond, the more readily they unite, mix, and accept one another.

Now, it is obvious that metals can be easily cast together with gold into a single mass, which other things—such as stone, wood, and herbs—cannot do. This is all a sign of the proximity of their natures to gold. Therefore, the Art <note>A common shorthand for Alchemy, the "Sacred Art" or "Great Work."</note> teaches how to transform the imperfect metals into gold, rather than other things like wood, herbs, and stone, because of the great difference and distant discord <note>original: *Zweytracht*. A philosophical term suggesting that the "internal frequencies" or natures of organic matter and gold are completely incompatible.</note> they have from the nature of gold.

A massive transformation <note>original: *Wandlung*</note> would have to occur within such things to bring them to such a nature and matter <note>original: *Materia*</note> that would be receptive to the Tincture and the forms of gold. If one could not find such matter already prepared by Nature within the imperfect metals, then this Art would be useless and in vain. But since we do find such matter prepared by Nature within the imperfect metals, the Art is indeed possible, having been made ready for it through the agency of Nature.

### In the Name of the Lord, Amen. <note>original: "In Nomine Domini Amen"</note>

Dearest son, know that the Spirit of the Lord, before the creation of heaven and earth, was carried or led upon the waters, as one reads in the Book of Genesis <note>original: "Buche der Schöpfunge," literally "Book of Creation"</note>. <margin>Note well <note>original: "Notabene"</note></margin> Now see that all things were created from the water, and God guided the water when He spoke and commanded a part of the water into the dry places; this He called the earth. And the water that He did not transform, He kept to moisten the earth. Why? Because a dry earth brings forth no fruit unless it is moistened by the water of the rain from above. Now I reveal to you, through natural conditions and distinctions in our undertaking, the <term>Stone of all Philosophers: the legendary Philosopher's Stone, believed to be the key to both physical transmutation and spiritual perfection</term> which is hidden. It is a stone adorned with a threefold garment: first, it is a stone of love and of wealth, and of elevation from all poverty and from all sickness. Within it is enclosed every secret given by God, and in the world there is no higher thing. You shall diligently note that I have said: our Stone is adorned with a threefold garment; that is, it shall <margin>Note well <note>original: "Notabene"</note></margin> be divided into three parts: into the **Body**, into the **Soul**, and into the **Spirit**. Therefore the body <note>original: "Leichnam," often implying a dead body or corpse in this context</note> is death, and does not have the soul

### No. 1.

## To make a phosphorus, which is at the same time a great medicine for humans and very useful in alchemy.

Take <note>original: "R.", the Latin abbreviation for "Recipe"</note> the urine of a young, strong, and healthy man—as many measures as you wish. Let it rot well in dung <note>a common alchemical practice using the steady, gentle heat of decomposing manure to facilitate fermentation</note>. Pour it into a large iron pan, though ensuring that at least three fingers' width of the pan remains empty, for otherwise it will boil over strongly in the fire, as it rises very easily. Place the pan with the urine over a charcoal fire and let it slowly boil down <note>the process of evaporation to concentrate the liquid</note> until it has become as hard as pitch, so that one can make balls out of it with one's hands that do not stick to the skin. Repeat this process with the remaining urine until it is all boiled down and made into balls.

<summary>This page provides the initial steps for creating a phosphorus compound from human urine, focusing on the fermentation and evaporation process to create a solid "pitch-like" base.</summary>
<keywords>phosphorus, alchemy, urine, medicinal preparation, evaporation, fermentation, charcoal fire</keywords>

--- Page 392 ---
<meta>This page continues the recipe for phosphorus from page 335, moving from the preparation of the urine "balls" to the distillation process in a retort.</meta>

Then take a suitable retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</note>, which must be two-thirds larger than the little balls that are to be put inside. Place the balls into it and set the retort in a sand bath <note>original: "Sandkapelle"; a container filled with sand that is heated to provide an even, controlled temperature to the glass vessel</note>, attaching a large receiver <note>a flask designed to collect the distilled liquid</note> to it, in which some water must have been placed beforehand. 

Then apply the first degree of heat, and the phlegm <note>the watery, inactive part of the substance</note> will pass over. When the spirits <note>the volatile, active vapors</note> begin to come, apply the second degree of heat, and continue in this manner until you notice oily drops. Then immediately remove this receiver and put another one in its place, which does not need to be as large as the first. Then apply the third degree of heat, and after two hours apply the strongest degree of heat using wood <note>referring to a high-intensity fire fueled by wood rather than just coals</note>, and then the oil will pass over entirely in the form of a dark yellow oil, mixed with all sorts of other colors. This oil is to be rectified <note>refined or purified through a second distillation</note> once by itself, so that if any phlegm or spirits were still present, they may be separated from it.

Take the retort in which the *dead head* <note>original: "Caput mortuum"; the solid residue or "dross" remaining after distillation</note> is found, and pour the rectified oil back onto it. Let it stand for 2 or 3 hours in *digestion* <note>a process of gentle, steady heating to soften or extract substances</note>; afterward, increase the heat degree by degree every 2 hours, and finally distill it over completely with wood and a flaming fire. This last operation is to be repeated three times.

stirring, let the lye evaporate entirely so that the saltpeter remains dry. Then repeat this process with the same saltpeter a second and also a third time.

Take a small piece of this prepared saltpeter, place it on a glowing coal, and if it does not hiss or burn, it is fixed <note>original: "fix"; in alchemy, a "fixed" substance is one that has become stable and non-volatile when exposed to heat, no longer evaporating or reacting violently</note>; but if it still burns, then this process must be repeated for a fourth time, and then it will be fixed.

## To disanimate Silver and make it compact.

## To *coagulate* *Mercury*.

Take a suitable crucible, fill it halfway with a good eggshell-lime that has been **calcined** <term>kalziniret<note>heated to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</note></term> three times; make a pit in the firmly pressed lime, fill it with running *mercury* <note>original: *Mercurio*</note>, and cover it with more of the same lime; let it sit in a **circulating fire** <term>Zirkelfeuer<note>a method of heating where the fire surrounds the vessel to ensure even heat from all sides</note></term> for 24 hours, increasing the intensity every 6 hours; then the *mercury* will be *compact* and can be hammered like the finest **silver** <term>$\text{\Moon}$<note>original symbol: ☽, the alchemical sign for silver</note></term>.

*This process has been tested and found to be untrue.* <note>The author or a later reader adds this skeptical post-script, warning that the recipe for turning mercury into silver does not work in practice.</note>

### No. 9.

## That Mercury Flows in Fire Like Wax.

Take fine <term>sublimated mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurium Sublimatum*, a chemical compound also known as corrosive sublimate</note>, dissolve it in a good <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: *Aquafort*, literally "strong water," referring to nitric acid</note>, using 4 <term>loths</term> <note>a historical German unit of weight, approximately 15 grams or half an ounce</note> of aqua fortis for every 1 loth of sublimate. In the aqua fortis, first dissolve 2 <term>loths</term> of <term>borax</term> <note>a mineral salt used in alchemy as a "flux" to help solids melt</note>, and then distill the aqua fortis away from it, using a strong fire at the very end; the mercury will remain at the bottom, yellow in color. Pour the aqua fortis back onto it and repeat this process five times. You will then have a mercury that is properly <term>fixed</term> <note>original: *fix*, a term for a substance that has been made stable and will no longer evaporate or "fly" when exposed to heat</note>, and as fluid as wax. If you are able to correctly <term>ferment</term> <note>in an alchemical context, this refers to the process of maturing a substance or "leavening" it with gold or silver to give it transmuting power</note> this mercury, you will have a certain <term>tincture</term> <note>the "Philosopher's Stone" in liquid or powdered form, capable of transforming base metals</note>, as surely as God and His holy Gospel help me.

NB. It is certain that if the aforementioned <term>mercury</term> is placed in a glass and it is <term>hermetically sealed</term> <note>original: *hermetisch verschlossen*, meaning the glass vessel's neck is melted and fused shut to be perfectly airtight</note>, it will flow in the fire like an oil without ceasing; however, if it is placed into an open fire in a crucible, it will vanish like a flash of lightning in an instant.

The <term>fermentation</term> mentioned by the author has not been tested, because it is not described within the process.

## No. 9.

## That Mercury May Flow in Fire Like Wax.

Take beautiful <term>mercury sublimat<gloss>mercuric chloride, a highly toxic and volatile white crystalline powder</gloss></term>, and dissolve it in a good <term>aqua fortis<gloss>literally "strong water"; nitric acid</gloss></term>, using 4 <term>loth<gloss>a historical German unit of weight, roughly 14.5 to 17.5 grams or half an ounce</gloss></term> of aqua fortis for every 1 loth of sublimat. Now take pure gold, which has been cast through **antimony** <note>original: "Antimonium"; this process was used to purify gold, as antimony reacts with and removes impurities</note> at least 3 or 4 times so that it becomes "fiery" <note>meaning highly purified or chemically reactive</note>; have it beaten into thin **leaves** <note>original: "folia"</note>. ## CHAPTER FOUR <note>original Latin: "CAPUT QUARTUM"</note>

### How one should proceed in particular with our Vitriol.

Finally, draw it off strongly and afterwards **reduce** <note>the process of heating a chemical residue back into its metallic form</note> the **silver calx** <note>original German: "Silberkalk"; the powdery residue or "ash" left after silver has been dissolved and the acid removed</note>; thus you will have the finest gold in all tests.

It will first become yellow, then fiery, and finally like scarlet. There you have now won the King of Honor and have worked it out to this point with much effort.

Then take out half of this; put the other half back in, thereafter <term>augment</term> <note>original: augmentire; the process of increasing the quantity or potency of the alchemical substance.</note> it again with 4 <term>Loth</term> of the oil, and let it pass through the colors, which operation you can repeat up to seven times.

With that which you have kept back, you can [transmute] gold, with one part [to] 16 parts <margin>Gold</margin>

If, however, one desires to work out the <term>quintessence<note>The "fifth essence"; the most purified and potent core of a substance, separated from its gross physical form.</note></term> from **vegetable matters**, such as from the swallow-wort called *Celandine* <note>original: "Chelidonia"</note>, as well as from rosemary, wormwood, and other herbs, I will likewise teach the **process** in detail, and herewith take up wormwood as the example.

### Observations on the preceding manuscript, which is said to be by Basilius Valentinus, wherein certain things must be observed in practice, without which the work will not succeed.

1st. Concerning the **mercury sublimate** <note>original: "Mercurii sublimati"; a toxic chemical compound of mercury and chlorine, often used as a reagent to facilitate chemical changes.</note>: Here, no common sort must be used, but rather the philosophical **Alcahest** <note>A hypothetical universal solvent in alchemy, capable of dissolving any substance into its primary matter.</note> or the "dry water of the wise," for common sublimate is too volatile.

2nd. Instead of distilled rainwater, a good distilled wine vinegar belongs here. No **mineral vinegar** <note>original: "Acetum minerale"; likely referring to a mineral acid like sulfuric acid.</note> is necessary here, because the **mineral acid** <note>original: "acidum minerale"</note> is already present from the mercury sublimate in the **vitriol** <note>original: "Vitriol"; a sulfate mineral, usually of iron or copper, prized for its corrosive and transformative properties.</note>.

3rdly. Regarding the work of the 2nd chapter: during **distillation** <term>Distillation: the process of heating a substance to create vapor and then cooling the vapor to collect the purified liquid.</term>, the following technique is primarily to be observed: namely, that the neck of the **retort** <term>Retort: a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances.</term> must be quite long, so that it reaches into the middle of the bulb of the **receiver** <term>Receiver: the glass vessel that collects the distilled substance at the end of the retort's neck.</term>, and the **red oil** <note>original: "rothe Oel"; a concentrated, often corrosive chemical essence.</note> falls into the **liquid** <note>original: "Liquor"</note> and not onto the glass; otherwise, it will burn a hole into the glass, as the oil is as heavy as lead and as hot as a glowing fire, which would result in nothing but damage and misfortune.

When the oil falls into the liquid, it makes such a noise as if a powerful **rocket** <note>original: "Rakette"</note> were being fired, which can greatly frighten the uninformed, but one need not fear any harm from this.

### SECOND CONJUNCTION
☿ ii

After the 7-fold <term>Aquilation</term> <note>original: "Aquilation"; an alchemical term for sublimation, named for the eagle (aquila) because the substance "flies" or rises to the top of the vessel</note> is finished, take the aforementioned <term>Regulus of Mercury</term> <note>original: "Regulum Mercurii"; the purified, metallic heart of the substance</note>, let it flow <note>melt</note> with a little **common salt** <note>original symbol: ⊖ commune</note> and 1 **ounce** <note>original symbol: ℥ j</note> of **Borax** for a quarter of an hour; repeat this 3 times so that the **dregs** <note>original: "feces"; the impurities or sediment</note> are removed and it is entirely purified. ### No. 23.

# To make a perfect Regulus of Mars.

Make a Regulus of Mars <term>Regulum martialem</term> <note>In alchemy, a "Regulus" is a metallic button or mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting. "Mars" is the alchemical code for iron. Thus, a Regulus of Mars is a metallic alloy of antimony and iron.</note> according to my method and save the slag <gloss>scoria</gloss>.

This Regulus is already animated by a part of the iron <note>original: "Martis"</note>, but it is still volatile.

Take this Regulus and pulverize it, mix in 2 parts of common sulfur, and let it flow in a crucible; in this way, the Regulus becomes antimony again as it was before, but of a far different form, because it now contains a fixed "martial soul" <note>The "soul" refers to the essential, non-volatile principle of the iron that has now been integrated into the antimony.</note> within itself.

Take this antimony and make a Regulus from it again using fresh iron, and proceed as described above, ensuring that the slag is saved each time.

You must repeat this 6, 7, or 8 times, or as often as you please; the more often it is done, the better, and you will eventually obtain a white Regulus that shines brilliantly like silver.

Take this Regulus <note>original: "König," literally "king"—an alchemical term for the metallic button found at the bottom of a crucible.</note>, pulverize it, and mix it with two parts of common sulfur, as stated above. Let it flow <note>i.e., melt in the crucible</note> so that the sulfur burns away entirely; in this way, you obtain an *antimony* as before.

Take this *antimony*, pulverize it, as well as all your saved slag <gloss>scoriae</gloss>, mix it all together and melt it; so you obtain a *Regulus*. Pulverize this, and mix in the remaining *slag*, let it all melt, and repeat this 3, 4, or 5 times. In this way, all the slag will turn into *Regulus*, so that finally all the *antimony* becomes a very penetrating and perfect *Regulus*. Save this for whatever use you desire.

Afterward, take **gold** and **Spanish ferretto** <note>original: "spanischen Ferretto," referring to copper calcined with sulfur or salt, used as a coloring agent.</note> (which is the same as if I said the modern-day **Venus** <note>Venus is the alchemical name for copper.</note>) <term>of each an equal amount</term>, let both flow together, and then add some of the above-mentioned <term>Aethiops</term> <note>The "mineral moor" or mercury-sulfur mixture prepared on the previous page.</note>. Note: However, ensure that with each melting, the **mercury** and **sulfur** smoke away and burn off entirely, until it no longer smokes.

If **silver** that has been refined by **saltpeter** for three periods of twenty-four hours is added to this **gold**, the **gold** recovers its natural color.

### No. 26.

# To transform silver into the finest gold.

Take a good parting-water <note>original: "Goldscheidewasser," a strong acid, usually nitric acid, used to separate gold from silver.</note> and dissolve <note>original: "solvir."</note> cupelled silver <note>silver purified through cupellation, a process of heating metal in a shallow porous cup to remove impurities.</note> in it; when it is dissolved, distill the aqua fortis <note>original: "Aquafort," Latin for "strong water," a corrosive mineral acid.</note> from it until it reaches dryness; wash <note>original: "süsse... aus," to edulcorate or rinse away acids and salts with water.</note> the silver calx <note>original: "Silberkalk," the metallic powder remaining after chemical treatment.</note> well with water and dry it. Then calcine <note>to heat to a high temperature without melting to effect a chemical change.</note> it with salt, so that the silver becomes quite loose and delicate.

Take 1 ounce of this and an equal amount of fresh mineral copper; let both flow together <note>melt into an alloy.</note> well, make small thin plates <note>original: "Lamellen."</note> from it, and cement <note>a process of heating metal plates packed in a powdered reagent.</note> these with cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide.</note> and alum; seal the crucible well so that nothing evaporates, place it in a circular fire <note>original: "Zirkelfeuer," a fire that surrounds the vessel to provide uniform, intense heat.</note> for 24 hours, increasing the heat every 6 hours; afterward, cupel it and part it, and you will receive a good portion of gold calx <note>gold in a powdered form.</note>.

## To Transform Silver into Fine Gold.

Take <term>Antimony</term> <note>original: *Antimonium*, a metallic element often used in alchemy to "purify" other metals</note> and <term>Saltpeter</term> in equal parts, as much as you wish; mix them well together, and let the mixture burn gradually and without delay in a glowing pot.

Then take that which has remained in the pot and grind it finely; put it into a glass and pour over it vinegar that has been distilled seven times, so that it covers the powder by a height of four fingers; distill this; but when it changes color, put another receiver <note>a collection vessel for the distillation process</note> in place, and thus you will obtain the <term>Oil of Antimony</term> <note>original: *Oleum Antimonii*</note>, which is to be set aside.

# How to Make the Oil of Egg Yolks.

Take egg yolks that have been boiled very hard and crush them in a mortar. Place this powder into a copper pan, set it over coals, and stir it diligently with a small wooden stick until the egg yolks have transformed into oil on their own; immediately press this through a linen cloth.

In this manner, you will obtain the oil of egg yolks, which is wonderful and black in color.

# How to Make the Incombustible Oil.

Take the *dead head* <note>original: *Caput mortuum*, the solid residue remaining after a substance has been distilled or heated to exhaustion</note> of soap and linseed oil in *equal parts* <note>original: *ana*, a medical and alchemical term indicating equal quantities</note>; then add an amount of white Venetian soap equal to the combined weight of the aforementioned *dead head* and linseed oil. Rub everything together well, and for every pound of the above ingredients, add 1 ounce of powdered *alkaline salt* <note>original: *Sal alcali*</note>. Form a dough from all of this and fill it into a *retort* <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</note>. Initially apply a gentle fire, but increase it *gradually* <note>original: *gradatim*</note> in proportion to the distillation; finally, apply the strongest fire until nothing more passes over.

## To make the Oil of Egg Yolks.

Take egg yolks that have been boiled very hard and crush them in a mortar. Place this powder into a small copper pan, set it upon coals, and stir it diligently with a small wooden stick for so long until the egg yolks have dissolved themselves into oil. Immediately press this through a linen cloth.

In this manner, you obtain the oil of egg yolks, which is wonderful and black in color.

## To make the incombustible Oil.

Take *dead head* <note>original: *Caput mortuum*; the solid residue remaining after a substance has been distilled or burned to exhaustion</note> from soap and linseed oil in equal parts <note>original: *ana*; a medical and alchemical term indicating equal quantities of the preceding ingredients</note>. Rub everything well together, and for every pound of the above ingredients, add 1 ounce of powdered *alkali salt* <note>original: *Sal alcali*; a basic salt, likely potash or soda ash, used as a reagent</note>. Make a dough from it all and fill it into a *retort* <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling chemicals</note>. At first, apply a gentle fire, but gradually <note>original: *gradatim*</note> increase the heat in proportion to the *distillation* process. At the very end, provide the strongest fire until nothing more passes over.

### No. 28.
## An excellent Lute.

Take white Venetian chalk, powder it finely, and then moisten it with enough <term>olive oil</term> <note>original: *Baumöl*; literally "tree oil," the historical German term for olive oil</note> so that a dough is made from it. This is kneaded very well, and then the *lute* <note>original: *Lutum*; a paste or cement used to seal the joints of chemical apparatus to prevent the escape of vapors</note> is finished. The glass vessels are sealed with this *lute*. It keeps the spirits <note>volatile vapors or essences</note> inside without loss, whether they be the very strongest <term>acids</term>, or the most volatile <term>alkaline salts</term> <note>original: *Laugensalze*</note>, or even the <term>mercurial spirits</term>; the *lute* remains soft at all times. If, however, it should become somewhat hard over time through the strength of the spirits, one needs only to moisten it again with a little <term>olive oil</term>.

But if you wish to have the Oil of Salt of Tartar <note>original: *Oleum salis tartari*; this is not a literal oil, but a concentrated liquid solution formed when the salt absorbs moisture from the air</note>, take the Salt of Tartar made fine in [Recipe] No. 3 and place it in a cellar; it will soon turn into an oil, which has great effects.

## No. 30.
### Coagulation of Mercury
<note>original: *Coagulatio Mercurii*; the process of "fixing" or solidifying liquid quicksilver</note>

Make an *aqua fortis* <term>Aquafort</term> <note>Literally "strong water," referring to nitric acid</note> from alum and saltpeter; when it has been distilled off, pour it back over the residue bit by bit. Moisten the "dead head" <term>Caput mortuum</term> <note>The solid chemical remains left over after distillation or sublimation</note> with the distilled liquid until it has absorbed all the strength of the *aqua fortis*. Then place it in the cellar and let it flow until it becomes an oil.

## No. 31.

# A Particular.
<note>A "Particular" refers to an alchemical procedure intended to produce a specific amount of gold or silver from a base metal, as opposed to a "Universal" work which seeks the Philosopher's Stone itself.</note>

Take crystals of niter <note>original: "Kristallen Nitri"; saltpeter or potassium nitrate</note> mixed with flowers of sulfur <term>flowers of sulfur: a fine yellow powder produced by the sublimation of sulfur</term> as much as suffices <note>original Latin: "q. s." for quantum satis</note>; dissolve this in a phlegm of vitriol <term>phlegm: a watery, weak distillate of a substance</term>, filter it, then draw off the liquid until it reaches dryness.

To 1 pound <note>original symbol: ℔</note> of the said liquid, add 2 pounds of dephlegmated <note>concentrated by removing the watery portion</note> spirit of vitriol <term>spirit of vitriol: sulfuric acid</term> into a flask, place a helm <note>the cap of a distillation apparatus, often called an alembic</note> upon it, and first apply a gentle fire until the phlegm has passed over. Then, strengthen the fire, so that the spirit of vitriol drives the spirit of niter <term>spirit of niter: nitric acid</term> over the helm in a blood-red color, and thus nothing of the niter remains behind. 

Continue with the fire until the helm becomes completely clear and white and no more drops fall; then the spirit of vitriol remains at the bottom <note>original Latin: "in fundo"</note> and flows like wax. However, when it is exposed to the air, it becomes a hard stone. If you place this stone in the fire, it flows like wax; if it comes into the open air, it coagulates <note>solidifies</note> once again.

### What follows is the Precipitated Mercury, which flows in the fire like a red ruby.

-> Take 2 Loth of live mercury. <term>live mercury: original: "Mercurium vivi"; liquid quicksilver</term> <-

# Of Various Unlucky Days.

### No. 36.

## D i g b y’ s  P r o c e s s.

Take 1 <term>lot <note>A historical German unit of weight, usually equivalent to about 15 to 16 grams.</note></term> of iron filings that have been washed clean and dried. Take one lot and a little bit more of gold, and dissolve it in <term>Aqua Regia</term>. Distill this solution also as many times as needed until the <term>Aqua Regia</term> remains as clear as if nothing had ever been in it; thus you will also obtain a pure solution of gold.

But in truth, the greatest Creator of all has imposed a specific <term>Character</term> <note>A spiritual mark, seal, or symbolic signature</note> and name upon every creature, as He is the one who counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names <note>original: "Ps. 146"; referring to Psalm 147:4 in modern Bibles: "He tells the number of the stars; he calls them all by their names."</note>. This aforementioned science was piously practiced by the ancient fathers, and even today, it is to be practiced by pious men.

For it was from this source that the sciences were revealed: Magic, <term>Cabala</term> <note>Kabbalah, a tradition of mystical interpretation and divine names</note>, and <term>Necromancy</term> <note>The art of conjuring spirits or the dead</note>. These later flourished significantly among the Egyptians, Persians, and Arabs, although they were used and corrupted in an abominable manner; men voluntarily surrendered themselves as slaves to evil demons through sacrilegious pacts, which is certainly a horrifying thing to hear. Because of this most evil purpose and abuse, this art was piously forbidden by the Church and secular authorities. Therefore, it is right that very few suitable books <note>The original Latin "liberos" likely intended "libros" (books), though it could literally mean "free men."</note> regarding its practice are to be found.

Therefore, this "Trumpet" <note>original: "Tubam"; likely a metaphorical name for the ritual method or the manuscript itself</note> of ours, which was obtained through special study, I deliver faithfully to you for the good...

<summary>The author justifies the use of divine names to command spirits, noting that even fallen angels retain their original celestial titles. He explains that while the magical arts originated with the "ancient fathers," they were later corrupted by pagan cultures, leading to their prohibition by the Church.</summary>

...however, <note>The text begins mid-word: "tamen" (however)</note> we do not wish this end to be shared or bequeathed for your destruction—which arises solely from abuse—but rather that you use it for your own good. For example, it may be used for uncovering hidden treasures, for journeys, for trade, for navigation, for war, and similar matters in which Spirits can be of benefit and service to you.

There are, moreover, other methods of summoning <term>vocatus</term> <note>A formal calling or invocation</note> or citations of Spirits which are performed through their highest princes, who hold authority among themselves. However, these spirits obey only with great difficulty and appear with an immense noise and clamor, taking on a most terrifying form, and not without great danger to the practitioner <term>operatoris</term> <note>The person performing the ritual</note>.

Therefore, this summoning of Spirits of ours, which we are about to describe, belongs specifically to Venus and is thus called by us the **Trumpet of Venus** <note>original: "Tuba Veneris"</note>, since almost all the evil demons are subject to the angels of the seven planets. Those spirits included in this little book are reckoned solely under the dominion of Venus; for this reason, the work has been titled by us the **Little Book of Venus** <note>original: "Libellus Veneris"</note>. Furthermore, the work is to be consecrated to this planet. We now begin its description and advise you to listen and attend to everything diligently. Farewell.

## CHAPTER ONE.

->*How the Seal or Symbol of Venus is to be completed.*<-

The first requirement for this necromantic <term>operation</term> <note>A ritual or magical procedure</note> of ours is the Seal of Venus <note>original: "Sigillum Veneris"</note>, which must be prepared in the following manner.

Take a piece of new copper <term>æris cupri</term> <note>The text specifies "new and never used" copper, the metal traditionally associated with the planet Venus</note> that has never been used before. From this, fashion a plate the size of the figure illustrated shortly hereafter. This plate must be cut according to the planet's own specific number—that is, with six angles <note>A hexagon; in traditional numerology, the number six is governed by Venus</note>. Then, using an iron or steel tool that is likewise new and clean, the Symbol <note>original: "Character"</note> should be engraved upon it. This must be done on the day of Venus <note>Friday</note> at night, during the third and tenth hours, counting from sunset. If the duration of one hour is not enough, you must wait until the other—that is, the tenth hour. However, it is only permitted to work during the hours of Venus <note>In planetary magic, specific hours of the day and night are assigned to the influence of the seven classical planets</note>, and indeed—which must be noted again—during the New Moon <note>original: "Novilunium"</note>. Therefore, if the Seal cannot be finished in a single Friday night during the two prescribed hours, you must similarly wait until the next New Moon.

After the Seal is finished, it should then be fumigated <note>Ritually cleansed or consecrated with smoke or incense</note> on that very same day and hour of Venus.

## CHAPTER TWO.

### *How the Trumpet of Venus is to be prepared.* <note>original: "Quomodo Tuba Veneris fit præparanda"</note>

Take a horn from a living bull. Then, take <term>Vitriol</term> <note>A metallic sulfate, often used as a cleaning agent or in alchemical preparations</note> dissolved in wine vinegar, with which the horn is to be washed and cleaned. Once this is done, the symbols <note>original: "characteres"</note> should be engraved into every part with the previously mentioned steel tool, just as they appear in the illustration that follows. However, this entire preparation of the horn, including the time in which it is taken from the bull (in the same manner as was indicated previously regarding the Seal), must be performed during the times, days, and hours of Venus <note>Friday, and specifically the hours of the day or night governed by the planet Venus</note>, which is important to note. Afterward, let it be fumigated and wrapped in a linen cloth; then, together with the Seal of Venus, let it be buried, dug up, and preserved for use.

## CHAPTER THREE.
### *How the Circle is to be Made.*

Before we proceed to the calling or summoning of spirits, we must discuss the construction of the <term>circle</term><note>The magic circle acts as a ritual boundary, separating the magician from the entities being summoned.</note>, as all <term>necromancers</term><note>In this historical context, "necromancy" refers broadly to ritual magic and the summoning of spirits, rather than strictly the modern definition of communicating with the dead.</note> always use them in their operations, protecting themselves through it as if through a most powerful fortification against the snares of demons.

The composition of circles is varied. Some practitioners working indoors create them with chalk, charcoal, and pigments. Some who perform <term>exorcisms</term><note>The act of "exorcising" here refers to the formal conjuration or commanding of spirits into a specific space.</note> in forests and groves make them with a sword or specific wooden staffs. Others, however, construct the circle from parchment, inscribed with divine names; this is the method we have chosen for our own operation. Just as we have left it already completed with all other requirements for a more fortunate heir, we also include here its form and the reasoning for it, to ensure the order and completeness of our little book.

Therefore, let <term>virgin parchment</term><note>Parchment or paper that has never been used for any other purpose, often symbolizing purity and readiness for spiritual inscription.</note> or paper be taken, and let circles the width of a thumb be cut from it.

CHAPTER FIVE.

### How this Little Book is to be consecrated. <note>original Latin: "Quomodo Libellus iste sit consecrandus"</note>

It is necessary that the little book, in which the names of the Spirits and the invocations are written, be consecrated beforehand, just as the ancient magi did. They established the consecration of similar books in such a way that they forced the spirits to appear immediately to anyone who simply opened the book; this, however, seems far too dangerous to us, especially if such a book should by misfortune fall into the hands of people entirely ignorant of this art. Therefore, it has pleased us to consecrate our little book in the following manner.

Let the Little Book be made from parchment, upon which first of all the character of <term>Venus</term> <note>indicated by the astronomical symbol ♀</note> shall be marked, and if one wishes, a certain image representing the figure of this Planet, with the sign of <term>Venus</term> above its head. Let the Little Book be prepared.
